bull_thesis:
Dürr is a 131-year-old German plant-engineering group that sells the paint shops and final-assembly lines car factories are built around, owns HOMAG (the world's largest maker of woodworking machinery), and owns two automation businesses. At 17.20 euros a share on the Frankfurt exchange it is valued at roughly 1.19 billion euros of equity and about 1.41 billion euros of enterprise value (equity plus net borrowings) against roughly 4.1 billion euros of annual revenue. That is about 0.35 times revenue and, on the company's own 2026 guidance, roughly seven times operating profit before one-off charges. For context, the closest listed comparison, Krones, trades today at 0.61 times revenue and 5.7 times operating profit before depreciation; Dürr sits below it on both.

The operating case rests on four things that are verifiable rather than hoped for. First, the Automotive division is a genuinely good business hiding inside a mediocre group. It earned an 11% operating margin in the fourth quarter of 2025, reported return on capital employed above 40%, derives roughly 28% of sales from servicing an installed base it alone can service, and is funded by customer prepayments rather than its own balance sheet. The demand argument management has made consistently since late 2024 holds up: customers "run a fleet of paint shops... that are very old and consume a lot of energy," and a paint shop is indifferent to whether the car it paints burns petrol or runs on a battery. Second, the self-help has landed. The group operating margin before one-off items rose from 4.6% to 5.6% in 2025 on slightly lower revenue, HOMAG lifted its margin by almost 200 basis points while its end market shrank, and a 50-million-euro administrative cost programme is running alongside about 30 million euros of recurring savings from the new Vector programme at the automation business. Third, management did what it said on the portfolio: five divisions became three on schedule, and the non-core environmental-technology business was sold on 31 October 2025 for gross proceeds of 290 to 310 million euros and an after-tax book profit of 227 million. Fourth, there is a new and credible growth pocket. The Schenck balancing business — the equipment that balances rotating parts, and on the chief executive's May 2025 account the equipment on which "nine out of 10 aircraft engines today are balanced" — grew orders, sales and earnings at double-digit rates in the first half of 2026 on aerospace and, explicitly, on "high energy demand for AI data centers."

The demand trough also looks like it has passed. Group order intake rose 13% in the second quarter of 2026 to 914 million euros, against a tariff-induced trough a year earlier, and management flagged a specific new tailwind: "increased project activity in the U.S. as foreign OEMs are speeding up CapEx plans there in order to increase local production and avoid tariffs." Geographic mix is rotating from a weak China and Germany toward India and Saudi Arabia. The balance sheet supports the wait — net borrowings of 218 million euros at 30 June 2026 against operating profit before depreciation of roughly 345 million — and the shares yield about 4.7% on the 0.80-euro dividend paid in the second quarter, which management explicitly defended in its August 2026 presentation.

The conditions this case requires: the Automotive margin holds near 9% through the European car industry's capital-spending squeeze; the second half of 2026 delivers the seasonal margin recovery management is guiding to; free cash flow turns positive again in 2027 once the payment pull-forward and the restructuring and tax cash-outs are behind it; and the proceeds of the environmental sale are not spent on another acquisition.
bear_thesis:
The reason this name screens as one of the cheapest industrials anywhere is that its two headline cheapness metrics are both artifacts, and correcting them removes roughly half the apparent bargain.

The reported 2025 earnings per share of 2.92, up 107%, is not operating profit — it is the 227-million-euro after-tax gain on selling the environmental-technology business. Profit from continuing operations in 2025 was negative 50 million euros. The trailing-twelve-month figure of 3.08 per share through 30 June 2026 carries the same gain: summing the four quarters gives +24.6 million, +260.0 million (the disposal), +20.2 million, and −89.5 million (a second write-down), for 215 million euros. Strip the disposal and add back the write-downs and the underlying run rate is roughly 75 to 85 million euros, or about 1.10 to 1.25 per share. Every valuation model fed by 2.92 or 3.08 — including the 37.12 "Buffett" fair value and the 46.30 discounted-cash-flow value — is inflated by roughly two and a half times at the input.

The 4.6 times price-to-free-cash-flow is the same problem in cash form. Trailing free cash flow of 225 million euros includes roughly 100 million euros of customer payments that arrived in December 2025 but belonged to 2026 — the finance chief said so plainly in March 2026: "you can roughly say that we received around 100 million more than we expected finally. And this, of course, is missing as a cash inflow in 2026." Full-year 2026 free-cash-flow guidance is negative 150 million euros to zero. First-half actual free cash flow was +58 million, so the second half is guided to somewhere between −208 million and −58 million, driven by that reversal plus tax on the environmental sale, restructuring cash-outs, and a disputed German tax audit whose size the company will not disclose. Net borrowings will likely rise from 218 million toward 350 to 400 million euros by December.

Underneath the accounting, the capital-allocation record is poor. Return on invested capital is 5.0%, below any reasonable cost of capital — this group does not compound, it re-rates or it does nothing. The BBS Automation acquisition, sold to investors in late 2024 as "building the second largest player in industrial automation," has been written down three times in five quarters: 120 million euros in the second quarter of 2025, 15 million in the battery business in the fourth, and 90 to 100 million more in the second quarter of 2026, leaving roughly 25 million of goodwill on a business bought for far more. The 2030 revenue target for it was cut by a quarter, from 800 million euros to "at least 600 million." Goodwill on the balance sheet fell from 520 million euros in March 2026 to 425 million in June 2026 in a single quarter.

The end markets give no near-term help. European car makers are cutting capital spending under existential competitive pressure. Management's own view of the electric-powertrain automation market is that the next investment wave will not begin "before the end of the decade" — a five-year hole in the segment sold as the growth engine. The furniture market that drives HOMAG has been weak for three consecutive years, and in March 2026 management said "it's still difficult to tell when there will be a real recovery." China, once a growth market, has declined for two years and management's explanation — competition, not exclusion — is an assertion the transcripts never evidence. And the medium-term plan itself was withdrawn for review in March 2026.

What would confirm the bear case: the second-half 2026 margin fails to deliver the seasonal recovery and the full year lands at or below the bottom of the 5.0-to-6.5% range; free cash flow comes in near the negative 150-million end of the guided range; Automotive order intake fails to convert the pipeline management calls "solid" into signed contracts in the fourth quarter; or the environmental-sale proceeds are spent on another acquisition rather than on debt and shareholders.
consensus_delta:
Where we disagree with the market runs in both directions here, and the more useful disagreement is with the value screens rather than with the sell side.

First, against the bulls and the screens. The published case for Dürr rests on a set of numbers that do not describe the business. The market data show earnings per share of 2.92 for 2025 (up 107%), trailing earnings of 3.08 through June 2026, and 4.6 times price-to-free-cash-flow. All three are artifacts. The 2025 profit is the 227-million-euro after-tax gain on selling the environmental-technology business; profit from continuing operations that year was negative 50 million euros. The trailing figure carries the same gain in its window. And the trailing free cash flow of 225 million euros contains roughly 100 million euros of customer payments that the finance chief said in March 2026 were pulled forward out of 2026. Anyone underwriting this at 4.6 times cash flow and a 114% margin of safety is underwriting a disposal and a payment-timing effect. On corrected numbers the business earns about 1.10 to 1.25 euros a share and trades near seven times operating profit on an enterprise-value basis — still cheap, but roughly half as cheap as advertised. This is the correction that matters most, and it is the reason this is a watchlist name rather than an entry.

Second, against the sell side, and in Dürr's favor. Nine analysts carry an average target of about 25.9 euros against a 17.20 price, so the street already sees the value; what it has not done is buy it, and the shares sit at 17.20 against a 52-week low of 16.76. The specific street assumption we think is wrong is the read-across from European car makers' distress to Dürr's order book. The reasoning is that if Volkswagen, Stellantis and their peers are cutting capital spending, their equipment suppliers must be cut proportionally. The transcripts contradict this on a specific mechanism management has repeated since November 2024: customers "run a fleet of paint shops... that are very old and consume a lot of energy and are very bad from an ESG perspective," so the spending is replacement and efficiency capital, not capacity capital, and it survives a capacity freeze. The order book supports the claim — group order intake rose 13% in the second quarter of 2026, and management named a driver the street has not modeled: "increased project activity in the U.S. as foreign OEMs are speeding up CapEx plans there in order to increase local production and avoid tariffs." Tariffs, which hurt Dürr through 2025 by freezing decisions, are now pulling forward American factory investment by foreign car makers, and Dürr sells into exactly that. A paint shop is also indifferent to powertrain, which decouples this revenue from the electric-vehicle transition debate that dominates the sector's rating.

Third, a piece of the business the market is not paying for at all. Schenck's balancing business grew orders, sales and earnings at double-digit rates in the first half of 2026 on aerospace and, in management's words, "high energy demand for AI data centers." That is a certified, installed-base niche — the chief executive's claim that "nine out of 10 aircraft engines today are balanced on our equipment" describes near-monopoly economics — sitting inside a reporting segment whose headline is dominated by BBS Automation's losses and write-downs. In our sum-of-the-parts it is worth roughly 330 million euros, or about 28% of the entire market capitalization, and nothing in the price suggests anyone is crediting it.
forcing_function:
For a value name with no live event, the honest answer is that there are two dated moments and one undated condition, and only the last of them actually forces a re-rating.

The two dated moments. The third-quarter 2026 trading statement, due in November, is the first check on whether the second-half margin recovery management is guiding to has arrived and whether the two or three large automotive orders described on 6 August as ones where "negotiations have progressed quite well" have been signed. Then the Capital Markets Day on 9-10 December 2026 at Bietigheim-Bissingen, where management said in March 2026 it would present a strategy update because it was "currently examining our midterm sales targets." That is a fixed date and it is the venue where a new medium-term margin target — the group has an 8% ambition it has never reached — would be set. But a Capital Markets Day is a presentation, not a binding commitment, and its asymmetry is genuinely two-sided: the first medium-term target management revisited in public, the 2030 revenue goal for BBS Automation, was cut by 25% on 6 August 2026. Buying ahead of it on the assumption that the reset is upward would be buying a coin flip.

The undated condition is the one that matters, and it is free cash flow turning positive again. Everything wrong with the market's view of this company is downstream of a cash flow line that is negative this year for four reasons that are all non-recurring: a payment pull-forward that reverses once, disposal tax paid once, restructuring cash paid once, and a tax-audit settlement paid once. When Dürr reports a year in which operating cash flow covers its spending — plausibly the 2027 guidance issued with full-year results in March 2027, and confirmed through 2027 itself — the entire funding-quality objection that this tape is currently penalising disappears, and a business earning roughly 200 to 240 million euros of operating profit will no longer be valued at 1.4 billion euros of enterprise value. That is the re-rating trigger. It is not dated, and it is roughly twelve to eighteen months away.

A fourth possibility, which we do not underwrite: a further portfolio action. Dürr has now shown it will sell a division at a good price, and BBS Automation, if Vector stabilises it, is an obvious candidate. Management has explicitly declined to signal this ("nothing to talk about at this moment" on non-core assets in May 2025, and on exiting the battery business, "Hard to rule anything out, but at the moment, that's not our plan"). It is optionality, not a plan.
valley_of_death:
The next three to nine months contain a specific, quantified, management-disclosed cash problem, and it lands before any of the good news does.

Full-year 2026 free cash flow is guided to between negative 150 million euros and zero. First-half actual free cash flow was positive 58 million, so the guidance implies a second half of somewhere between minus 208 million and minus 58 million. Four things drive it, and management named each: the roughly 100 million euros of customer payments that arrived in December 2025 instead of 2026 and now leave a hole; the tax due on the environmental-technology disposal, which was booked as a gain in 2025 but paid in cash in 2026; restructuring cash-outs from the Vector programme, of which 40 to 50 million euros of the total 140-to-150-million charge is cash and mostly falls in the second half; and a disputed German tax audit that the company is taking to court and whose size it explicitly refuses to disclose ("we don't want to mention the number due to the tax authority not letting to know our real position on this"). That last item is an undisclosed cash liability of unknown magnitude — the single largest unquantified risk in the file.

The arithmetic consequence is that net borrowings rise from 218 million euros at 30 June 2026 toward 350 to 400 million by December, on top of the 55 million euros of dividends already paid in the second quarter. This is not a solvency problem — leverage would still be roughly one times operating profit before depreciation, funding is described as comfortable, and the 150-million-euro convertible bond that matured in January 2026 has already been dealt with. It is a sentiment problem, and it is squarely on the wrong side of what this market is currently rewarding. The regime read for August 2026 is explicit that the tape has re-priced companies on funding quality — businesses whose cash flow covers their spending were bought and businesses with negative free cash flow were sold — and that it did so with the long end of the yield curve at a nineteen-year high, so the discount rate applied to any story that pays off later keeps rising even as the Federal Reserve stops being the reason. A German industrial guiding to negative free cash flow into that tape is not a name the market will re-rate on the strength of its sum-of-the-parts. UPDATE 2026-09-22: this mechanism strengthened rather than reversed since the anchor -- the ECB (9/10), Fed (9/16) and BOJ (9/18) all hiked inside the same nine days and the US 10-year printed its first close at or above 5% since 2007, so the discount-rate headwind this section describes is now live on three fronts rather than one.

There is a second, softer hazard. The margin guidance of 5.0 to 6.5% for 2026 was already walked toward "the lower area of the guidance" on 6 August, with the second quarter at 4.3%. Dürr's business is seasonally back-half weighted and the whole year now depends on a fourth quarter delivering what the fourth quarter of 2025 delivered (a 7.4% margin). If the two or three large automotive orders management says are close to signing slip into 2027 — and management itself warned that "predicting the timing of contract awards continues to be a challenge" — both the margin and the order-intake guidance come under pressure at the same moment, in the November trading statement, right before the December Capital Markets Day.
positioning_washout:
There is no forced, mechanical selling event of the kind that creates a clean entry, and investors waiting for one should know that.

The dividend, which would be the obvious trigger for a yield-focused holder base to liquidate, is not being cut. Dürr paid 55.4 million euros, or 0.80 euros a share, in the second quarter of 2026, and the August 2026 investor presentation went out of its way to state that a "strong balance sheet and multi-year cash-generation allow for sustainable dividends." That is a deliberate signal, made in the same year free cash flow is guided negative, and it should be read as a commitment rather than a hope. The 4.7% yield at 17.20 euros therefore holds, which supports the shareholder register rather than shaking it.

What has already happened instead is a slower, quieter de-rating. The shares are at 17.20 against a 52-week high of 25.10 and a low of 16.76 — roughly 7% up from the bottom of the year's range, 5% below the 50-day average and 16% below the 200-day. The market capitalization of 1.19 billion euros is below the SDAX-scale threshold that keeps generalist European small-cap funds interested, and average daily volume is under 100,000 shares, so the register is thinning by attrition rather than by a single event. The 7-out-of-100 smart-money score and a zero insider buy ratio say what they say: nobody with an information advantage, inside or outside the company, is stepping in. In a name where management has just written down an acquisition for the third time, the absence of any insider purchase at a 52-week low is a meaningful non-signal.

The one mechanical dynamic worth naming is on the other side of the ledger. HOMAG's remaining minority holders — roughly 2.55 million shares, about 16% of that subsidiary — sit under a control and profit-transfer agreement with a court-set guaranteed dividend of 1.19 euros a share and a settlement price of 31.58 euros, fixed by the Stuttgart Higher Regional Court in December 2024. That is a small, capped, known liability of roughly 80 million euros, not an overhang. It is the reason Dürr already takes essentially all of HOMAG's profit, and it removes any risk that a minority buyout becomes a surprise cash call.

A capitulation low is possible if the November trading statement disappoints on both margin and orders, but it is not scheduled and it will not be mechanical. It would be ordinary disappointment selling, and it is the specific development worth waiting for. UPDATE 2026-09-22: the shares are now AT the 52-week low (16.40, versus 16.76 at the anchor), still on no company-specific news and still with no insider buying reported -- the quiet de-rating this section describes has continued rather than reversed, and the wait for the November trading statement remains the operative plan, not a mechanical washout.

bull_thesis:
Dürr is a 131-year-old German plant-engineering group that sells the paint shops and final-assembly lines car factories are built around, owns HOMAG (the world's largest maker of woodworking machinery), and owns two automation businesses. At 17.20 euros a share on the Frankfurt exchange it is valued at roughly 1.19 billion euros of equity and about 1.41 billion euros of enterprise value (equity plus net borrowings) against roughly 4.1 billion euros of annual revenue. That is about 0.35 times revenue and, on the company's own 2026 guidance, roughly seven times operating profit before one-off charges. For context, the closest listed comparison, Krones, trades today at 0.61 times revenue and 5.7 times operating profit before depreciation; Dürr sits below it on both.

The operating case rests on four things that are verifiable rather than hoped for. First, the Automotive division is a genuinely good business hiding inside a mediocre group. It earned an 11% operating margin in the fourth quarter of 2025, reported return on capital employed above 40%, derives roughly 28% of sales from servicing an installed base it alone can service, and is funded by customer prepayments rather than its own balance sheet. The demand argument management has made consistently since late 2024 holds up: customers "run a fleet of paint shops... that are very old and consume a lot of energy," and a paint shop is indifferent to whether the car it paints burns petrol or runs on a battery. Second, the self-help has landed. The group operating margin before one-off items rose from 4.6% to 5.6% in 2025 on slightly lower revenue, HOMAG lifted its margin by almost 200 basis points while its end market shrank, and a 50-million-euro administrative cost programme is running alongside about 30 million euros of recurring savings from the new Vector programme at the automation business. Third, management did what it said on the portfolio: five divisions became three on schedule, and the non-core environmental-technology business was sold on 31 October 2025 for gross proceeds of 290 to 310 million euros and an after-tax book profit of 227 million. Fourth, there is a new and credible growth pocket. The Schenck balancing business — the equipment that balances rotating parts, and on the chief executive's May 2025 account the equipment on which "nine out of 10 aircraft engines today are balanced" — grew orders, sales and earnings at double-digit rates in the first half of 2026 on aerospace and, explicitly, on "high energy demand for AI data centers."

The demand trough also looks like it has passed. Group order intake rose 13% in the second quarter of 2026 to 914 million euros, against a tariff-induced trough a year earlier, and management flagged a specific new tailwind: "increased project activity in the U.S. as foreign OEMs are speeding up CapEx plans there in order to increase local production and avoid tariffs." Geographic mix is rotating from a weak China and Germany toward India and Saudi Arabia. The balance sheet supports the wait — net borrowings of 218 million euros at 30 June 2026 against operating profit before depreciation of roughly 345 million — and the shares yield about 4.7% on the 0.80-euro dividend paid in the second quarter, which management explicitly defended in its August 2026 presentation.

The conditions this case requires: the Automotive margin holds near 9% through the European car industry's capital-spending squeeze; the second half of 2026 delivers the seasonal margin recovery management is guiding to; free cash flow turns positive again in 2027 once the payment pull-forward and the restructuring and tax cash-outs are behind it; and the proceeds of the environmental sale are not spent on another acquisition.
bear_thesis:
The reason this name screens as one of the cheapest industrials anywhere is that its two headline cheapness metrics are both artifacts, and correcting them removes roughly half the apparent bargain.

The reported 2025 earnings per share of 2.92, up 107%, is not operating profit — it is the 227-million-euro after-tax gain on selling the environmental-technology business. Profit from continuing operations in 2025 was negative 50 million euros. The trailing-twelve-month figure of 3.08 per share through 30 June 2026 carries the same gain: summing the four quarters gives +24.6 million, +260.0 million (the disposal), +20.2 million, and −89.5 million (a second write-down), for 215 million euros. Strip the disposal and add back the write-downs and the underlying run rate is roughly 75 to 85 million euros, or about 1.10 to 1.25 per share. Every valuation model fed by 2.92 or 3.08 — including the 37.12 "Buffett" fair value and the 46.30 discounted-cash-flow value — is inflated by roughly two and a half times at the input.

The 4.6 times price-to-free-cash-flow is the same problem in cash form. Trailing free cash flow of 225 million euros includes roughly 100 million euros of customer payments that arrived in December 2025 but belonged to 2026 — the finance chief said so plainly in March 2026: "you can roughly say that we received around 100 million more than we expected finally. And this, of course, is missing as a cash inflow in 2026." Full-year 2026 free-cash-flow guidance is negative 150 million euros to zero. First-half actual free cash flow was +58 million, so the second half is guided to somewhere between −208 million and −58 million, driven by that reversal plus tax on the environmental sale, restructuring cash-outs, and a disputed German tax audit whose size the company will not disclose. Net borrowings will likely rise from 218 million toward 350 to 400 million euros by December.

Underneath the accounting, the capital-allocation record is poor. Return on invested capital is 5.0%, below any reasonable cost of capital — this group does not compound, it re-rates or it does nothing. The BBS Automation acquisition, sold to investors in late 2024 as "building the second largest player in industrial automation," has been written down three times in five quarters: 120 million euros in the second quarter of 2025, 15 million in the battery business in the fourth, and 90 to 100 million more in the second quarter of 2026, leaving roughly 25 million of goodwill on a business bought for far more. The 2030 revenue target for it was cut by a quarter, from 800 million euros to "at least 600 million." Goodwill on the balance sheet fell from 520 million euros in March 2026 to 425 million in June 2026 in a single quarter.

The end markets give no near-term help. European car makers are cutting capital spending under existential competitive pressure. Management's own view of the electric-powertrain automation market is that the next investment wave will not begin "before the end of the decade" — a five-year hole in the segment sold as the growth engine. The furniture market that drives HOMAG has been weak for three consecutive years, and in March 2026 management said "it's still difficult to tell when there will be a real recovery." China, once a growth market, has declined for two years and management's explanation — competition, not exclusion — is an assertion the transcripts never evidence. And the medium-term plan itself was withdrawn for review in March 2026.

What would confirm the bear case: the second-half 2026 margin fails to deliver the seasonal recovery and the full year lands at or below the bottom of the 5.0-to-6.5% range; free cash flow comes in near the negative 150-million end of the guided range; Automotive order intake fails to convert the pipeline management calls "solid" into signed contracts in the fourth quarter; or the environmental-sale proceeds are spent on another acquisition rather than on debt and shareholders.
consensus_delta:
Where we disagree with the market runs in both directions here, and the more useful disagreement is with the value screens rather than with the sell side.

First, against the bulls and the screens. The published case for Dürr rests on a set of numbers that do not describe the business. The market data show earnings per share of 2.92 for 2025 (up 107%), trailing earnings of 3.08 through June 2026, and 4.6 times price-to-free-cash-flow. All three are artifacts. The 2025 profit is the 227-million-euro after-tax gain on selling the environmental-technology business; profit from continuing operations that year was negative 50 million euros. The trailing figure carries the same gain in its window. And the trailing free cash flow of 225 million euros contains roughly 100 million euros of customer payments that the finance chief said in March 2026 were pulled forward out of 2026. Anyone underwriting this at 4.6 times cash flow and a 114% margin of safety is underwriting a disposal and a payment-timing effect. On corrected numbers the business earns about 1.10 to 1.25 euros a share and trades near seven times operating profit on an enterprise-value basis — still cheap, but roughly half as cheap as advertised. This is the correction that matters most, and it is the reason this is a watchlist name rather than an entry.

Second, against the sell side, and in Dürr's favor. Nine analysts carry an average target of about 25.9 euros against a 17.20 price, so the street already sees the value; what it has not done is buy it, and the shares sit at 17.20 against a 52-week low of 16.76. The specific street assumption we think is wrong is the read-across from European car makers' distress to Dürr's order book. The reasoning is that if Volkswagen, Stellantis and their peers are cutting capital spending, their equipment suppliers must be cut proportionally. The transcripts contradict this on a specific mechanism management has repeated since November 2024: customers "run a fleet of paint shops... that are very old and consume a lot of energy and are very bad from an ESG perspective," so the spending is replacement and efficiency capital, not capacity capital, and it survives a capacity freeze. The order book supports the claim — group order intake rose 13% in the second quarter of 2026, and management named a driver the street has not modeled: "increased project activity in the U.S. as foreign OEMs are speeding up CapEx plans there in order to increase local production and avoid tariffs." Tariffs, which hurt Dürr through 2025 by freezing decisions, are now pulling forward American factory investment by foreign car makers, and Dürr sells into exactly that. A paint shop is also indifferent to powertrain, which decouples this revenue from the electric-vehicle transition debate that dominates the sector's rating.

Third, a piece of the business the market is not paying for at all. Schenck's balancing business grew orders, sales and earnings at double-digit rates in the first half of 2026 on aerospace and, in management's words, "high energy demand for AI data centers." That is a certified, installed-base niche — the chief executive's claim that "nine out of 10 aircraft engines today are balanced on our equipment" describes near-monopoly economics — sitting inside a reporting segment whose headline is dominated by BBS Automation's losses and write-downs. In our sum-of-the-parts it is worth roughly 330 million euros, or about 28% of the entire market capitalization, and nothing in the price suggests anyone is crediting it.
forcing_function:
For a value name with no live event, the honest answer is that there are two dated moments and one undated condition, and only the last of them actually forces a re-rating.

The two dated moments. The third-quarter 2026 trading statement, due in November, is the first check on whether the second-half margin recovery management is guiding to has arrived and whether the two or three large automotive orders described on 6 August as ones where "negotiations have progressed quite well" have been signed. Then the Capital Markets Day on 9-10 December 2026 at Bietigheim-Bissingen, where management said in March 2026 it would present a strategy update because it was "currently examining our midterm sales targets." That is a fixed date and it is the venue where a new medium-term margin target — the group has an 8% ambition it has never reached — would be set. But a Capital Markets Day is a presentation, not a binding commitment, and its asymmetry is genuinely two-sided: the first medium-term target management revisited in public, the 2030 revenue goal for BBS Automation, was cut by 25% on 6 August 2026. Buying ahead of it on the assumption that the reset is upward would be buying a coin flip.

The undated condition is the one that matters, and it is free cash flow turning positive again. Everything wrong with the market's view of this company is downstream of a cash flow line that is negative this year for four reasons that are all non-recurring: a payment pull-forward that reverses once, disposal tax paid once, restructuring cash paid once, and a tax-audit settlement paid once. When Dürr reports a year in which operating cash flow covers its spending — plausibly the 2027 guidance issued with full-year results in March 2027, and confirmed through 2027 itself — the entire funding-quality objection that this tape is currently penalising disappears, and a business earning roughly 200 to 240 million euros of operating profit will no longer be valued at 1.4 billion euros of enterprise value. That is the re-rating trigger. It is not dated, and it is roughly twelve to eighteen months away.

A fourth possibility, which we do not underwrite: a further portfolio action. Dürr has now shown it will sell a division at a good price, and BBS Automation, if Vector stabilises it, is an obvious candidate. Management has explicitly declined to signal this ("nothing to talk about at this moment" on non-core assets in May 2025, and on exiting the battery business, "Hard to rule anything out, but at the moment, that's not our plan"). It is optionality, not a plan.
valley_of_death:
The next three to nine months contain a specific, quantified, management-disclosed cash problem, and it lands before any of the good news does.

Full-year 2026 free cash flow is guided to between negative 150 million euros and zero. First-half actual free cash flow was positive 58 million, so the guidance implies a second half of somewhere between minus 208 million and minus 58 million. Four things drive it, and management named each: the roughly 100 million euros of customer payments that arrived in December 2025 instead of 2026 and now leave a hole; the tax due on the environmental-technology disposal, which was booked as a gain in 2025 but paid in cash in 2026; restructuring cash-outs from the Vector programme, of which 40 to 50 million euros of the total 140-to-150-million charge is cash and mostly falls in the second half; and a disputed German tax audit that the company is taking to court and whose size it explicitly refuses to disclose ("we don't want to mention the number due to the tax authority not letting to know our real position on this"). That last item is an undisclosed cash liability of unknown magnitude — the single largest unquantified risk in the file.

The arithmetic consequence is that net borrowings rise from 218 million euros at 30 June 2026 toward 350 to 400 million by December, on top of the 55 million euros of dividends already paid in the second quarter. This is not a solvency problem — leverage would still be roughly one times operating profit before depreciation, funding is described as comfortable, and the 150-million-euro convertible bond that matured in January 2026 has already been dealt with. It is a sentiment problem, and it is squarely on the wrong side of what this market is currently rewarding. The regime read for August 2026 is explicit that the tape has re-priced companies on funding quality — businesses whose cash flow covers their spending were bought and businesses with negative free cash flow were sold — and that it did so with the long end of the yield curve at a nineteen-year high, so the discount rate applied to any story that pays off later keeps rising even as the Federal Reserve stops being the reason. A German industrial guiding to negative free cash flow into that tape is not a name the market will re-rate on the strength of its sum-of-the-parts. positioning_washout:
There is no forced, mechanical selling event of the kind that creates a clean entry, and investors waiting for one should know that.

The dividend, which would be the obvious trigger for a yield-focused holder base to liquidate, is not being cut. Dürr paid 55.4 million euros, or 0.80 euros a share, in the second quarter of 2026, and the August 2026 investor presentation went out of its way to state that a "strong balance sheet and multi-year cash-generation allow for sustainable dividends." That is a deliberate signal, made in the same year free cash flow is guided negative, and it should be read as a commitment rather than a hope. The 4.7% yield at 17.20 euros therefore holds, which supports the shareholder register rather than shaking it.

What has already happened instead is a slower, quieter de-rating. The shares are at 17.20 against a 52-week high of 25.10 and a low of 16.76 — roughly 7% up from the bottom of the year's range, 5% below the 50-day average and 16% below the 200-day. The market capitalization of 1.19 billion euros is below the SDAX-scale threshold that keeps generalist European small-cap funds interested, and average daily volume is under 100,000 shares, so the register is thinning by attrition rather than by a single event. The 7-out-of-100 smart-money score and a zero insider buy ratio say what they say: nobody with an information advantage, inside or outside the company, is stepping in. In a name where management has just written down an acquisition for the third time, the absence of any insider purchase at a 52-week low is a meaningful non-signal.

The one mechanical dynamic worth naming is on the other side of the ledger. HOMAG's remaining minority holders — roughly 2.55 million shares, about 16% of that subsidiary — sit under a control and profit-transfer agreement with a court-set guaranteed dividend of 1.19 euros a share and a settlement price of 31.58 euros, fixed by the Stuttgart Higher Regional Court in December 2024. That is a small, capped, known liability of roughly 80 million euros, not an overhang. It is the reason Dürr already takes essentially all of HOMAG's profit, and it removes any risk that a minority buyout becomes a surprise cash call.

A capitulation low is possible if the November trading statement disappoints on both margin and orders, but it is not scheduled and it will not be mechanical. It would be ordinary disappointment selling, and it is the specific development worth waiting for. moderator_conclusion:
Dürr is a real bargain wearing a fake price tag, and the right response is to wait for a better entry rather than to buy the tag.

Start with what is true. This is a 131-year-old business that is the world's largest supplier of automotive paint shops, owns the world's largest woodworking-machinery maker, and owns a balancing business on which — by its own chief executive's account — nine out of ten aircraft engines are balanced. Its Automotive division earned an 11% operating margin in the fourth quarter of 2025 and reports return on capital employed above 40%, funded by customer prepayments rather than its own balance sheet. Management has done what it said: five divisions became three on schedule, the non-core environmental business was sold on 31 October 2025 at a 227-million-euro after-tax gain, the group operating margin rose 100 basis points to 5.6% on falling revenue, and HOMAG lifted its own margin by nearly 200 basis points while its end market shrank for a third straight year. At 17.20 euros a share the whole thing is valued at about 0.35 times revenue and around seven times operating profit, against a nearest listed comparison, Krones, at 0.61 times revenue. Our sum-of-the-parts, built division by division on 2026 guided earnings and today's de-rated peer ratings, comes to about 24.50 euros a share — roughly 42% above the price, and close to the published analyst consensus of about 25.9 euros reached independently.

Now the correction, which is why this is not an entry today. The reason Dürr appears on a deep-value screen at 4.6 times cash flow with a 114% margin of safety is that both inputs are artifacts. The 2025 earnings per share of 2.92, up 107%, is the disposal gain — continuing operations lost 50 million euros that year — and the trailing 3.08 through June 2026 carries the same gain in its window. The trailing free cash flow of 225 million euros includes roughly 100 million of customer payments the finance chief openly said were pulled forward out of 2026. Correct both and the business earns about 1.10 to 1.25 euros a share and is guided to burn cash this year, with full-year free cash flow between negative 150 million and zero. It is still cheap. It is cheap by about half as much as the screen says, and a position sized on the screen's version of the arithmetic would be sized wrong.

The forensic record adds a second reservation. Three goodwill write-downs in five quarters on one acquisition — 120 million euros in the second quarter of 2025, 15 million in the fourth, and 90 to 100 million more in the second quarter of 2026 — have erased roughly 235 million euros of value from a business bought at the peak of the electric-vehicle equipment wave, whose 2030 revenue target has now been cut by a quarter. Return on invested capital of 5.0% says the group as a whole does not compound. This is a re-rating trade on a narrow-moat collection of good divisions and one bad one, not a compounder to be held through anything.

The timing call is straightforward once the regime is applied. This tape has just re-priced companies on funding quality — cash-covering businesses bought, negative-free-cash-flow businesses sold — with the long end of the yield curve at a nineteen-year high, which keeps raising the discount rate on anything that pays off later. Dürr will report negative free cash flow this year, will carry an undisclosed German tax-audit settlement through it, and has already walked its margin guidance toward the lower end with the second quarter at 4.3%. That is a live driver working against the position, not a spent one, and it argues for patience. The catalyst question is separate and, in this book, neutral: the one binding event already happened and its money is banked, which neither helps nor hurts the residual value case.

So: watchlist, not entry. Three specific things would move this to a buy, any one of which suffices. First, price — at or below roughly 15 euros the shares would trade at about 0.85 times book and around five and a half times operating profit on 2026 guidance, which pays for the cash-flow year in advance. Second, the November trading statement showing the second-half margin recovery arriving and one or more of the large automotive contracts signed, which would confirm the earnings base underneath our sum-of-the-parts. Third, the 9-10 December Capital Markets Day resetting credible medium-term margin targets with the automation drag properly ring-fenced. Absent one of those, the value is real, the price is close, and the calendar is against it.

Separately, on the value case alone — ignoring the catalyst position and the regime entirely, and judging only price against our fair value and the quality of the numbers — this rates a 4 out of 5. The discount to a division-by-division valuation is large enough to qualify, the moat is narrow but being defended rather than eroded, and the terminal-value threat is material rather than fatal because paint shops are indifferent to powertrain and global vehicle production is relocating rather than disappearing. What holds it back from a 5 is the forensic quality: the trailing earnings and trailing cash flow that anchor the case are both one-off artifacts, and a management team that has written down the same acquisition three times in five quarters has not yet earned the benefit of the doubt on the asset values that remain.

- Unallocated holding-company cost of about 20 million euros a year capitalized at 8 times: minus 160 million euros.
Enterprise value: 2,070 million euros.
Less net borrowings of 218 million euros (30 June 2026, borrowings of 992 million less cash of 774 million; this is the figure excluding capitalized leases, which is how the company's own filings usually present it), pension and similar provisions of about 90 million, and the HOMAG minority claim of about 80 million euros.
Equity value 1,682 million euros over 69.2 million shares = 24.31 euros, rounded to 24.50.

Cross-check: at 24.50 a share the enterprise value would be about 1,913 million euros, or 0.47 times revenue and 5.5 times profit before depreciation — just below Krones at 0.61 times and 5.7 times, and far below GEA Group at 1.92 times and 11.9 times. That is a deliberately unheroic rating, and it lands close to the published analyst consensus target of roughly 25.9 euros from nine analysts, reached by a different route.
risk_reward: From 17.20 euros: the adverse case at 13.00 and the base case at 24.50. There is no structural floor under the price — no deal terms, no tender, no net cash position (the company carries net borrowings of 218 million euros), and a 4.7% dividend yield is a payout policy, not a floor. The honest statement of the setup is that a bad European capital-spending year takes this to roughly three-quarters of book value, and a normal one takes it to a rating still below its closest listed peer.
peer_comps_note:
The peer group is German plant-engineering and capital-equipment makers exposed to the same industrial capital-spending cycle, plus the direct woodworking-machinery comparison. I anchored to live multiples pulled today rather than remembered ones, which matters here because the peer set has itself de-rated hard.

As of 24 August 2026: GEA Group trades at 1.92 times revenue and 11.9 times operating profit before depreciation, with return on capital employed of 19.5%; Krones at 0.61 times revenue and 5.7 times, with return on capital employed of 12.9%; Biesse at 0.22 times revenue and 6.4 times, with return on capital employed of 2.2% and a loss on the year. Krones is 6% below its 200-day average and Biesse is 37% below its 52-week high, so the anchor I am using is already a shocked one. Dürr at 17.20 euros trades at about 0.35 times revenue and 3.8 times operating profit before depreciation.

So Dürr is cheap on this comparison, but the size of the gap needs two corrections. First, GEA is not a fair anchor — it earns nearly four times Dürr's return on invested capital in food and pharmaceutical process technology, and its rating belongs to that quality, not to auto-shop plant engineering. Krones is the honest anchor, and against Krones the discount is roughly a third, not a half. Second, and more important, part of this gap is shared-factor sector beta rather than anything specific to Dürr: all four names are levered to the same unresolved driver, European industrial and automotive capital spending, and all four have de-rated together on it. I do not credit that portion as name-specific edge. What is genuinely idiosyncratic to Dürr is a lower rating than Krones on a comparable return on capital employed guidance of 13 to 18%, plus a divisional mix (Automotive at above 40% return on capital employed, Schenck in a certified aerospace niche) that is better than the group average implies.

One correction to the peer file's own rationale: it rests on "unanimous MoS agreement plus an earnings inflection." The earnings inflection it cites — earnings per share up 107% on falling revenue — is the environmental-technology disposal gain, not operating leverage, and the discounted-cash-flow, Graham and owner-earnings margins of safety are all computed from that polluted earnings figure. The relative-value conclusion survives on enterprise-value-to-revenue and enterprise-value-to-profit-before-depreciation; the earnings-based half of it does not.

bull_thesis:
Dürr is a 131-year-old German plant-engineering group that sells the paint shops and final-assembly lines car factories are built around, owns HOMAG (the world's largest maker of woodworking machinery), and owns two automation businesses. At 17.20 euros a share on the Frankfurt exchange it is valued at roughly 1.19 billion euros of equity and about 1.41 billion euros of enterprise value (equity plus net borrowings) against roughly 4.1 billion euros of annual revenue. That is about 0.35 times revenue and, on the company's own 2026 guidance, roughly seven times operating profit before one-off charges. For context, the closest listed comparison, Krones, trades today at 0.61 times revenue and 5.7 times operating profit before depreciation; Dürr sits below it on both.

The operating case rests on four things that are verifiable rather than hoped for. First, the Automotive division is a genuinely good business hiding inside a mediocre group. It earned an 11% operating margin in the fourth quarter of 2025, reported return on capital employed above 40%, derives roughly 28% of sales from servicing an installed base it alone can service, and is funded by customer prepayments rather than its own balance sheet. The demand argument management has made consistently since late 2024 holds up: customers "run a fleet of paint shops... that are very old and consume a lot of energy," and a paint shop is indifferent to whether the car it paints burns petrol or runs on a battery. Second, the self-help has landed. The group operating margin before one-off items rose from 4.6% to 5.6% in 2025 on slightly lower revenue, HOMAG lifted its margin by almost 200 basis points while its end market shrank, and a 50-million-euro administrative cost programme is running alongside about 30 million euros of recurring savings from the new Vector programme at the automation business. Third, management did what it said on the portfolio: five divisions became three on schedule, and the non-core environmental-technology business was sold on 31 October 2025 for gross proceeds of 290 to 310 million euros and an after-tax book profit of 227 million. Fourth, there is a new and credible growth pocket. The Schenck balancing business — the equipment that balances rotating parts, and on the chief executive's May 2025 account the equipment on which "nine out of 10 aircraft engines today are balanced" — grew orders, sales and earnings at double-digit rates in the first half of 2026 on aerospace and, explicitly, on "high energy demand for AI data centers."

The demand trough also looks like it has passed. Group order intake rose 13% in the second quarter of 2026 to 914 million euros, against a tariff-induced trough a year earlier, and management flagged a specific new tailwind: "increased project activity in the U.S. as foreign OEMs are speeding up CapEx plans there in order to increase local production and avoid tariffs." Geographic mix is rotating from a weak China and Germany toward India and Saudi Arabia. The balance sheet supports the wait — net borrowings of 218 million euros at 30 June 2026 against operating profit before depreciation of roughly 345 million — and the shares yield about 4.7% on the 0.80-euro dividend paid in the second quarter, which management explicitly defended in its August 2026 presentation.

The conditions this case requires: the Automotive margin holds near 9% through the European car industry's capital-spending squeeze; the second half of 2026 delivers the seasonal margin recovery management is guiding to; free cash flow turns positive again in 2027 once the payment pull-forward and the restructuring and tax cash-outs are behind it; and the proceeds of the environmental sale are not spent on another acquisition.
bear_thesis:
The reason this name screens as one of the cheapest industrials anywhere is that its two headline cheapness metrics are both artifacts, and correcting them removes roughly half the apparent bargain.

The reported 2025 earnings per share of 2.92, up 107%, is not operating profit — it is the 227-million-euro after-tax gain on selling the environmental-technology business. Profit from continuing operations in 2025 was negative 50 million euros. The trailing-twelve-month figure of 3.08 per share through 30 June 2026 carries the same gain: summing the four quarters gives +24.6 million, +260.0 million (the disposal), +20.2 million, and −89.5 million (a second write-down), for 215 million euros. Strip the disposal and add back the write-downs and the underlying run rate is roughly 75 to 85 million euros, or about 1.10 to 1.25 per share. Every valuation model fed by 2.92 or 3.08 — including the 37.12 "Buffett" fair value and the 46.30 discounted-cash-flow value — is inflated by roughly two and a half times at the input.

The 4.6 times price-to-free-cash-flow is the same problem in cash form. Trailing free cash flow of 225 million euros includes roughly 100 million euros of customer payments that arrived in December 2025 but belonged to 2026 — the finance chief said so plainly in March 2026: "you can roughly say that we received around 100 million more than we expected finally. And this, of course, is missing as a cash inflow in 2026." Full-year 2026 free-cash-flow guidance is negative 150 million euros to zero. First-half actual free cash flow was +58 million, so the second half is guided to somewhere between −208 million and −58 million, driven by that reversal plus tax on the environmental sale, restructuring cash-outs, and a disputed German tax audit whose size the company will not disclose. Net borrowings will likely rise from 218 million toward 350 to 400 million euros by December.

Underneath the accounting, the capital-allocation record is poor. Return on invested capital is 5.0%, below any reasonable cost of capital — this group does not compound, it re-rates or it does nothing. The BBS Automation acquisition, sold to investors in late 2024 as "building the second largest player in industrial automation," has been written down three times in five quarters: 120 million euros in the second quarter of 2025, 15 million in the battery business in the fourth, and 90 to 100 million more in the second quarter of 2026, leaving roughly 25 million of goodwill on a business bought for far more. The 2030 revenue target for it was cut by a quarter, from 800 million euros to "at least 600 million." Goodwill on the balance sheet fell from 520 million euros in March 2026 to 425 million in June 2026 in a single quarter.

The end markets give no near-term help. European car makers are cutting capital spending under existential competitive pressure. Management's own view of the electric-powertrain automation market is that the next investment wave will not begin "before the end of the decade" — a five-year hole in the segment sold as the growth engine. The furniture market that drives HOMAG has been weak for three consecutive years, and in March 2026 management said "it's still difficult to tell when there will be a real recovery." China, once a growth market, has declined for two years and management's explanation — competition, not exclusion — is an assertion the transcripts never evidence. And the medium-term plan itself was withdrawn for review in March 2026.

What would confirm the bear case: the second-half 2026 margin fails to deliver the seasonal recovery and the full year lands at or below the bottom of the 5.0-to-6.5% range; free cash flow comes in near the negative 150-million end of the guided range; Automotive order intake fails to convert the pipeline management calls "solid" into signed contracts in the fourth quarter; or the environmental-sale proceeds are spent on another acquisition rather than on debt and shareholders.
consensus_delta:
Where we disagree with the market runs in both directions here, and the more useful disagreement is with the value screens rather than with the sell side.

First, against the bulls and the screens. The published case for Dürr rests on a set of numbers that do not describe the business. The market data show earnings per share of 2.92 for 2025 (up 107%), trailing earnings of 3.08 through June 2026, and 4.6 times price-to-free-cash-flow. All three are artifacts. The 2025 profit is the 227-million-euro after-tax gain on selling the environmental-technology business; profit from continuing operations that year was negative 50 million euros. The trailing figure carries the same gain in its window. And the trailing free cash flow of 225 million euros contains roughly 100 million euros of customer payments that the finance chief said in March 2026 were pulled forward out of 2026. Anyone underwriting this at 4.6 times cash flow and a 114% margin of safety is underwriting a disposal and a payment-timing effect. On corrected numbers the business earns about 1.10 to 1.25 euros a share and trades near seven times operating profit on an enterprise-value basis — still cheap, but roughly half as cheap as advertised. This is the correction that matters most, and it is the reason this is a watchlist name rather than an entry.

Second, against the sell side, and in Dürr's favor. Nine analysts carry an average target of about 25.9 euros against a 17.20 price, so the street already sees the value; what it has not done is buy it, and the shares sit at 17.20 against a 52-week low of 16.76. The specific street assumption we think is wrong is the read-across from European car makers' distress to Dürr's order book. The reasoning is that if Volkswagen, Stellantis and their peers are cutting capital spending, their equipment suppliers must be cut proportionally. The transcripts contradict this on a specific mechanism management has repeated since November 2024: customers "run a fleet of paint shops... that are very old and consume a lot of energy and are very bad from an ESG perspective," so the spending is replacement and efficiency capital, not capacity capital, and it survives a capacity freeze. The order book supports the claim — group order intake rose 13% in the second quarter of 2026, and management named a driver the street has not modeled: "increased project activity in the U.S. as foreign OEMs are speeding up CapEx plans there in order to increase local production and avoid tariffs." Tariffs, which hurt Dürr through 2025 by freezing decisions, are now pulling forward American factory investment by foreign car makers, and Dürr sells into exactly that. A paint shop is also indifferent to powertrain, which decouples this revenue from the electric-vehicle transition debate that dominates the sector's rating.

Third, a piece of the business the market is not paying for at all. Schenck's balancing business grew orders, sales and earnings at double-digit rates in the first half of 2026 on aerospace and, in management's words, "high energy demand for AI data centers." That is a certified, installed-base niche — the chief executive's claim that "nine out of 10 aircraft engines today are balanced on our equipment" describes near-monopoly economics — sitting inside a reporting segment whose headline is dominated by BBS Automation's losses and write-downs. In our sum-of-the-parts it is worth roughly 330 million euros, or about 28% of the entire market capitalization, and nothing in the price suggests anyone is crediting it.
forcing_function:
For a value name with no live event, the honest answer is that there are two dated moments and one undated condition, and only the last of them actually forces a re-rating.

The two dated moments. The third-quarter 2026 trading statement, due in November, is the first check on whether the second-half margin recovery management is guiding to has arrived and whether the two or three large automotive orders described on 6 August as ones where "negotiations have progressed quite well" have been signed. Then the Capital Markets Day on 9-10 December 2026 at Bietigheim-Bissingen, where management said in March 2026 it would present a strategy update because it was "currently examining our midterm sales targets." That is a fixed date and it is the venue where a new medium-term margin target — the group has an 8% ambition it has never reached — would be set. But a Capital Markets Day is a presentation, not a binding commitment, and its asymmetry is genuinely two-sided: the first medium-term target management revisited in public, the 2030 revenue goal for BBS Automation, was cut by 25% on 6 August 2026. Buying ahead of it on the assumption that the reset is upward would be buying a coin flip.

The undated condition is the one that matters, and it is free cash flow turning positive again. Everything wrong with the market's view of this company is downstream of a cash flow line that is negative this year for four reasons that are all non-recurring: a payment pull-forward that reverses once, disposal tax paid once, restructuring cash paid once, and a tax-audit settlement paid once. When Dürr reports a year in which operating cash flow covers its spending — plausibly the 2027 guidance issued with full-year results in March 2027, and confirmed through 2027 itself — the entire funding-quality objection that this tape is currently penalising disappears, and a business earning roughly 200 to 240 million euros of operating profit will no longer be valued at 1.4 billion euros of enterprise value. That is the re-rating trigger. It is not dated, and it is roughly twelve to eighteen months away.

A fourth possibility, which we do not underwrite: a further portfolio action. Dürr has now shown it will sell a division at a good price, and BBS Automation, if Vector stabilises it, is an obvious candidate. Management has explicitly declined to signal this ("nothing to talk about at this moment" on non-core assets in May 2025, and on exiting the battery business, "Hard to rule anything out, but at the moment, that's not our plan"). It is optionality, not a plan.
valley_of_death:
The next three to nine months contain a specific, quantified, management-disclosed cash problem, and it lands before any of the good news does.

Full-year 2026 free cash flow is guided to between negative 150 million euros and zero. First-half actual free cash flow was positive 58 million, so the guidance implies a second half of somewhere between minus 208 million and minus 58 million. Four things drive it, and management named each: the roughly 100 million euros of customer payments that arrived in December 2025 instead of 2026 and now leave a hole; the tax due on the environmental-technology disposal, which was booked as a gain in 2025 but paid in cash in 2026; restructuring cash-outs from the Vector programme, of which 40 to 50 million euros of the total 140-to-150-million charge is cash and mostly falls in the second half; and a disputed German tax audit that the company is taking to court and whose size it explicitly refuses to disclose ("we don't want to mention the number due to the tax authority not letting to know our real position on this"). That last item is an undisclosed cash liability of unknown magnitude — the single largest unquantified risk in the file.

The arithmetic consequence is that net borrowings rise from 218 million euros at 30 June 2026 toward 350 to 400 million by December, on top of the 55 million euros of dividends already paid in the second quarter. This is not a solvency problem — leverage would still be roughly one times operating profit before depreciation, funding is described as comfortable, and the 150-million-euro convertible bond that matured in January 2026 has already been dealt with. It is a sentiment problem, and it is squarely on the wrong side of what this market is currently rewarding. The regime read for August 2026 is explicit that the tape has re-priced companies on funding quality — businesses whose cash flow covers their spending were bought and businesses with negative free cash flow were sold — and that it did so with the long end of the yield curve at a nineteen-year high, so the discount rate applied to any story that pays off later keeps rising even as the Federal Reserve stops being the reason. A German industrial guiding to negative free cash flow into that tape is not a name the market will re-rate on the strength of its sum-of-the-parts. positioning_washout:
There is no forced, mechanical selling event of the kind that creates a clean entry, and investors waiting for one should know that.

The dividend, which would be the obvious trigger for a yield-focused holder base to liquidate, is not being cut. Dürr paid 55.4 million euros, or 0.80 euros a share, in the second quarter of 2026, and the August 2026 investor presentation went out of its way to state that a "strong balance sheet and multi-year cash-generation allow for sustainable dividends." That is a deliberate signal, made in the same year free cash flow is guided negative, and it should be read as a commitment rather than a hope. The 4.7% yield at 17.20 euros therefore holds, which supports the shareholder register rather than shaking it.

What has already happened instead is a slower, quieter de-rating. The shares are at 17.20 against a 52-week high of 25.10 and a low of 16.76 — roughly 7% up from the bottom of the year's range, 5% below the 50-day average and 16% below the 200-day. The market capitalization of 1.19 billion euros is below the SDAX-scale threshold that keeps generalist European small-cap funds interested, and average daily volume is under 100,000 shares, so the register is thinning by attrition rather than by a single event. The 7-out-of-100 smart-money score and a zero insider buy ratio say what they say: nobody with an information advantage, inside or outside the company, is stepping in. In a name where management has just written down an acquisition for the third time, the absence of any insider purchase at a 52-week low is a meaningful non-signal.

The one mechanical dynamic worth naming is on the other side of the ledger. HOMAG's remaining minority holders — roughly 2.55 million shares, about 16% of that subsidiary — sit under a control and profit-transfer agreement with a court-set guaranteed dividend of 1.19 euros a share and a settlement price of 31.58 euros, fixed by the Stuttgart Higher Regional Court in December 2024. That is a small, capped, known liability of roughly 80 million euros, not an overhang. It is the reason Dürr already takes essentially all of HOMAG's profit, and it removes any risk that a minority buyout becomes a surprise cash call.

A capitulation low is possible if the November trading statement disappoints on both margin and orders, but it is not scheduled and it will not be mechanical. It would be ordinary disappointment selling, and it is the specific development worth waiting for. moderator_conclusion:
Dürr is a real bargain wearing a fake price tag, and the right response is to wait for a better entry rather than to buy the tag.

Start with what is true. This is a 131-year-old business that is the world's largest supplier of automotive paint shops, owns the world's largest woodworking-machinery maker, and owns a balancing business on which — by its own chief executive's account — nine out of ten aircraft engines are balanced. Its Automotive division earned an 11% operating margin in the fourth quarter of 2025 and reports return on capital employed above 40%, funded by customer prepayments rather than its own balance sheet. Management has done what it said: five divisions became three on schedule, the non-core environmental business was sold on 31 October 2025 at a 227-million-euro after-tax gain, the group operating margin rose 100 basis points to 5.6% on falling revenue, and HOMAG lifted its own margin by nearly 200 basis points while its end market shrank for a third straight year. At 17.20 euros a share the whole thing is valued at about 0.35 times revenue and around seven times operating profit, against a nearest listed comparison, Krones, at 0.61 times revenue. Our sum-of-the-parts, built division by division on 2026 guided earnings and today's de-rated peer ratings, comes to about 24.50 euros a share — roughly 42% above the price, and close to the published analyst consensus of about 25.9 euros reached independently.

Now the correction, which is why this is not an entry today. The reason Dürr appears on a deep-value screen at 4.6 times cash flow with a 114% margin of safety is that both inputs are artifacts. The 2025 earnings per share of 2.92, up 107%, is the disposal gain — continuing operations lost 50 million euros that year — and the trailing 3.08 through June 2026 carries the same gain in its window. The trailing free cash flow of 225 million euros includes roughly 100 million of customer payments the finance chief openly said were pulled forward out of 2026. Correct both and the business earns about 1.10 to 1.25 euros a share and is guided to burn cash this year, with full-year free cash flow between negative 150 million and zero. It is still cheap. It is cheap by about half as much as the screen says, and a position sized on the screen's version of the arithmetic would be sized wrong.

The forensic record adds a second reservation. Three goodwill write-downs in five quarters on one acquisition — 120 million euros in the second quarter of 2025, 15 million in the fourth, and 90 to 100 million more in the second quarter of 2026 — have erased roughly 235 million euros of value from a business bought at the peak of the electric-vehicle equipment wave, whose 2030 revenue target has now been cut by a quarter. Return on invested capital of 5.0% says the group as a whole does not compound. This is a re-rating trade on a narrow-moat collection of good divisions and one bad one, not a compounder to be held through anything.

The timing call is straightforward once the regime is applied. This tape has just re-priced companies on funding quality — cash-covering businesses bought, negative-free-cash-flow businesses sold — with the long end of the yield curve at a nineteen-year high, which keeps raising the discount rate on anything that pays off later. Dürr will report negative free cash flow this year, will carry an undisclosed German tax-audit settlement through it, and has already walked its margin guidance toward the lower end with the second quarter at 4.3%. That is a live driver working against the position, not a spent one, and it argues for patience. The catalyst question is separate and, in this book, neutral: the one binding event already happened and its money is banked, which neither helps nor hurts the residual value case.

So: watchlist, not entry. Three specific things would move this to a buy, any one of which suffices. First, price — at or below roughly 15 euros the shares would trade at about 0.85 times book and around five and a half times operating profit on 2026 guidance, which pays for the cash-flow year in advance. Second, the November trading statement showing the second-half margin recovery arriving and one or more of the large automotive contracts signed, which would confirm the earnings base underneath our sum-of-the-parts. Third, the 9-10 December Capital Markets Day resetting credible medium-term margin targets with the automation drag properly ring-fenced. Absent one of those, the value is real, the price is close, and the calendar is against it.

Separately, on the value case alone — ignoring the catalyst position and the regime entirely, and judging only price against our fair value and the quality of the numbers — this rates a 4 out of 5. The discount to a division-by-division valuation is large enough to qualify, the moat is narrow but being defended rather than eroded, and the terminal-value threat is material rather than fatal because paint shops are indifferent to powertrain and global vehicle production is relocating rather than disappearing. What holds it back from a 5 is the forensic quality: the trailing earnings and trailing cash flow that anchor the case are both one-off artifacts, and a management team that has written down the same acquisition three times in five quarters has not yet earned the benefit of the doubt on the asset values that remain.
